newsitem.title: COTE D'IVOIRE: Donors want tougher forest policy in Ivory Coast.
newsitem.headline: Donors want tougher forest policy in Ivory Coast.

text.p: Aid donors are withholding funds from Ivory Coast's forestry agency, partly because it has failed to halt illegal tree-felling in protected forests, donor sources say.
Another major reason is that it has failed to meet wood production targets while preserving the forest stock through replanting programmes.
Since donors provide all the resources of the Societe de Developpement des Forets (SODEFOR), the agency says it may be forced to make up to 300 workers redundant out of a workforce of 1,200.
One aid official, who declined to be named, said the government's forestry plan for the years 1988-96 had shown mixed results at best.
It had failed completely to meet its production target -- four million cubic metres (141 million cubic feet) of timber per year while preserving the forest stock.

"Currently, production is falling rapidly, with two million cubic metres produced in 1996, and SODEFOR reckons that resources in the normal forests, those without special protection, are going to disappear rapidly over the next three or four years," he added.
Total forest area in Ivory Coast has decreased to around 3.9 million hectares (9.6 million acres) from 12 million hectares (29.7 million acres) before independence in 1957.

"This is a very serious situation for Ivory Coast -- the disappearance of a resource that provided a strong contribution to its gross domestic product, its exports and its trade balance," the donor source said.
Timber exports totalled an estimated $400 million in 1995, making it Ivory Coast's second biggest export behind cocoa, which brought in over $1 billion.

The situation is no better concerning forests deemed "protected". By some estimates, 30 percent of such forests have been illegally occupied by up to 450,000 cocoa and coffee planters, and illegal clearing by slash-and-burn farmers continues despite warnings from the authorities.

"You can still see in the forests clearing operations going on, in particular by people who've settled there illegally, and that's worrying, in that it's a socio-economic phenomenon that seems uncontrollable," said another donor official recently returned from a field visit.

Donors have finally lost patience and are pressing the government to come up with more effective policies involving sanctions if rules are flouted and tax benefits to encourage protection of rare tree species.

SODEFOR managing director Jean-Claude Anoh told the opposition La Voie newspaper on Tuesday that a World Bank project ended last December, and an African Development Bank project would finish at the end of this year.
Only German funding was left, under a programme scheduled to continue until 2002.

Anoh, according to La Voie, confirmed a reduction in operations, even if only temporary until donor money returned, would mean the loss of between 250 and 300 jobs. Some people would leave on early retirement and some would have to be found other jobs because they had civil servant status, he added.
